items.title: The New AI Superpowers: Focus and Followthrough [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The New AI Superpowers: Focus and Followthrough
items.summary:
The article discusses how AI's ability to accelerate task completion paradoxically contributes to burnout by enabling people to start many projects simultaneously without finishing them. The author reflects on personal experience, noting that despite AI increasing productivity, the finite nature of human time and energy means that spreading oneself too thin leads to exhaustion rather than relief.

The author advocates for a strategy of focusing deeply on fewer projects and following through thoroughly, rather than expanding the number of tasks. Drawing on concepts from essentialism and the analogy of a total versus partial eclipse, the article emphasizes the value of dedicating effort to achieve high-quality outcomes. The piece concludes that AI should be used to save time and enhance focus, helping people avoid burnout and produce more meaningful work.

items.title: Researchers develop hybrid probabilistic forecasting system combining time series and NLP to predict roadblocks in Bolivia, improving accuracy over traditional models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Seasonality to Semantics: Benchmarking a Hybrid Probabilistic Forecasting System for Roadblocks in Bolivia
items.summary:
Roadblocks in Bolivia cause significant economic losses estimated at 4% of GDP, yet local predictive systems have been lacking. This study presents a hybrid forecasting system that integrates time series decomposition with natural language processing of six years of Bolivian news to detect early signals of social tension leading to roadblocks. The system was tested over 1,762 days across seven forecasting horizons and outperformed statistical models like SARIMA and LightGBM, achieving an AUC-ROC of 0.677 at the shortest horizon and reducing prediction error significantly.

The methodology uses vector semantic embeddings and zero-shot classification to capture discursive escalation before roadblocks occur. Validation showed consistent error reduction across all horizons, demonstrating that incorporating semantic news signals can detect social tension peaks missed by historical data alone. This approach offers a technical tool for risk management in critical transport corridors affected by social conflicts in Bolivia.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.21785v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Roadblocks in Bolivia are a social conflict phenomenon with devastating economic impacts, estimated at losses equivalent to 4% of the national Gross Domestic Product. Despite their recurrence and impact, there is a lack of local predictive systems to anticipate these events for logistical decision-making. This paper presents a hybrid probabilistic forecasting system that integrates time series decomposition (Prophet) with natural language processing (NLP) techniques applied to a six-year corpus of Bolivian news coverage. The methodology employs vector semantic embeddings and zero-shot classification models to capture signals of discursive escalation prior to the materialization of the roadblocks. Using an expanding walk-forward validation scheme applied over 1,762 days and seven forecasting horizons (H+1 to H+7), seven internal configurations and four external benchmarks were compared, including SARIMA and LightGBM. The results demonstrate that the hybrid configuration (Prophet + NLP, C6) consistently outperforms purely statistical models, achieving an AUC-ROC of 0.677 at H+1 and reducing the Brier Score by 10.9% relative to the baseline temporal model (0.220 vs. 0.247), maintaining a statistically significant error reduction across all evaluated horizons ($p < 0.02$). This research validates that the integration of semantic news signals allows for the detection of social tension peaks not captured by historical inertia, providing a technical tool for risk management in critical transport corridors.

items.title: LeAct introduces a method to recover natural-language reasoning from expert system actions, improving AI reasoning across games and robotics benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LeAct: Learning to Reason from Expert Actions
items.summary: LeAct (Learning to reason from Actions) is a new approach that extracts latent chains of thought from expert systems, which typically produce optimal actions without explaining their reasoning. By sampling candidate reasoning paths and selecting those that improve action recovery, LeAct enables AI models to learn from expert actions and generalize beyond them. The method achieves near-optimal performance on small games, outperforms expert-iteration baselines by five times on larger scales, and improves training on a robotics benchmark where direct imitation falls short. This framework positions expert systems as a novel source of reasoning supervision for foundation models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.21856v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern reasoning models depend on reasoning data, today sourced from human annotations or distilled from stronger LLMs. However, a rich and largely untapped source of supervision lies in expert systems (e.g., game engines, classical planners, theorem provers), which routinely produce near-optimal actions across diverse domains. But these experts are silent: they commit to an action without writing down the chain of thought (CoT) behind it. Recovering that CoT as natural-language reasoning would distill expert knowledge into a student that generalizes beyond the demonstrated actions. We treat it as a latent variable and study how to recover it from the action alone. Our approach, LeAct (Learning to reason from Actions), optimizes this latent variable: the student samples candidate CoTs for each expert action, and we retain those that measurably improve its own probability of recovering the action. Across imperfect-information games at multiple scales and a simulated robotics benchmark, LeAct reaches the solver's numerical floor on small enumerable games. At larger scale, it is $5\times$ closer to the solver than the strongest expert-iteration baseline. At Flop Hold'em ($\sim 10^9$ infosets), LeAct wins head-to-head by $+60$ mbb/g, and on the robotics probe it is the only training recipe that improves on direct imitation. We present a principled framework and the result: expert systems become a categorically new source of reasoning teachers for foundation models.

items.title: MetaEvolve framework trains LLMs to develop self-evolution meta-skills via reinforcement learning on coding tasks, improving performance by up to 46.9% on out-of-distribution benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Teaching LLMs to Self-Evolve: Cultivating Core Meta-Skills with Reinforcement Learning
items.summary:
Researchers present MetaEvolve, a framework that cultivates meta-skills like self-reflection and iterative refinement in large language models through a data synthesis pipeline, evolution-aware reinforcement learning, and evolutionary search at inference time. The approach leverages program execution as a continuous reward signal to train models on large-scale code data, aiming to generalize these skills beyond coding to open-ended problems.

MetaEvolve was evaluated across seven coding benchmarks, outperforming the strongest baseline by 10.01% on in-distribution tasks and 24.12% on out-of-distribution tasks. It also achieved a 46.9% relative improvement on algorithm optimization problems outside the training domain, demonstrating that explicitly training self-evolution meta-skills can enhance AI autonomy and capability.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.21971v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Test-time scaling through iterative self-evolution with environment feedback, as demonstrated by AlphaEvolve, shows remarkable performance gains. We hypothesize that the success of such evolution frameworks hinges on meta-skills, such as self-reflection with environment feedback, that enable effective multi-round refinement, yet are largely neglected by traditional post-training. To bridge this gap, we present MetaEvolve, a framework designed to develop these meta-skills via a data synthesis pipeline, evolution-aware reinforcement learning (RL), and inference-time evolutionary search. Concretely, we ground MetaEvolve in coding, where program execution provides natural, continuous reward signals beyond binary correctness. Building on these signals, we synthesize evolution trajectories as training data, each containing a current program, its fitness score (combining correctness and efficiency), and a history of prior attempts, and train the model via RL with verifiable rewards derived from test case execution. By training on large-scale code data, we aim to inspire generalizable domain-agnostic meta-skills that can transfer broadly to open-ended problems where such rich training signals are scarce. Across seven coding benchmarks, MetaEvolve outperforms the strongest baseline by 10.01% absolute on in-distribution tasks and 24.12% on out-of-distribution tasks. On open-ended algorithm optimization problems entirely outside the training domain, it further achieves a 46.9% relative improvement. These results demonstrate that explicitly cultivating self-evolution meta-skills offers a principled path toward more capable and autonomously self-evolving AI.

items.title: Researchers present DBA-Bench, a production-fidelity benchmark for evaluating LLM-based database operations agents across 106 scenarios with PostgreSQL environments [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: DBA-Bench: A Production-Fidelity Benchmark for LLM-Based Database Operations Agents
items.summary:
Researchers introduce DBA-Bench, a benchmark designed to address gaps in evaluating large language model (LLM)-based database agents by simulating production-like environments with multi-turn interactions, complex observations, and multiple remediation options. The benchmark includes 106 scenarios across seven task domains using instrumented PostgreSQL setups with active workloads and persistent states, defining success by measurable recovery or fault elimination under safety constraints.

The study evaluates nine baseline groups, including foundation models, GPT-5.5-backed agents, and a human database administrator (DBA) reference, across 848 automated runs. Results show automated agents achieve Diagnosis, Outcome, and Safe Pass rates of 32.7%, 19.6%, and 12.4%, respectively, with the best automated Safe Pass rate at 17.9% compared to 93.4% for the human DBA. Performance declines on harder scenarios, highlighting challenges in safe end-to-end remediation by automated systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.22165v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM-based database agents show promise, but differing task scopes, testbeds, and metrics hinder comparison. We identify four gaps between evaluation and production operations: live-environment fidelity (multi-turn read-write interaction with a running database); observation-space scale and complexity (causal diagnosis across thousands of time series, business logs, and concurrent activity); solution-space openness (multiple remediations with different operational trade-offs); and scenario complexity and coverage (faults cascading across internal mechanisms and operational domains). We present DBA-Bench, a benchmark addressing these gaps through production fidelity, outcome-first evaluation, and controlled scenario reproducibility. It uses instrumented PostgreSQL environments with active workloads, persistent state, and multi-source observations; defines success by measurable recovery or fault elimination under safety constraints; and restores snapshots with scenario-specific checks before each run. The benchmark contains 106 scenarios across seven task domains, with two public difficulty labels based on reference-path diagnostic depth and environmental complexity. We evaluate nine baseline groups, including six foundation-model systems, two GPT-5.5-backed database agents, and a Human DBA reference. Across 848 automated runs, Diagnosis, Outcome, and Safe Pass rates are 32.7%, 19.6%, and 12.4%; the best automated baseline reaches 17.9% Safe Pass versus 93.4% for the Human DBA reference. Automated Safe Pass falls from 19.6% on Easy scenarios to 7.6% on Hard scenarios, underscoring the difficulty of safe end-to-end remediation.

items.title: Researchers introduce Byte-Prefix Marginalization for cross-tokenizer on-policy distillation, improving student model training across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Cross-Tokenizer On-Policy Distillation via Byte-Prefix Marginalization
items.summary: Researchers propose Byte-Prefix Marginalization (BPM), a method that re-expresses a teacher language model's next-token distribution over a student model's vocabulary in a shared byte space, preserving probability mass and aligning tokenization. BPM assigns teacher token probabilities to the longest student token whose byte representation prefixes the teacher token's bytes, aggregating mass and handling unmatched mass explicitly, enabling vocabulary-complete and mass-preserving targets for on-policy distillation without requiring shared tokenizers. Evaluated on models including Qwen3-32B, GLM-Z1-9B-0414, and MiniMax-M2.7, BPM outperforms existing cross-tokenizer methods on six mathematics and programming benchmarks, improving average scores by 3.7 to 6.6 points over the strongest baselines.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.22334v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open-weight language models from different families exhibit complementary capabilities, motivating their consolidation into a compact student through on-policy distillation (OPD). However, full-vocabulary OPD typically assumes a shared tokenizer, while existing cross-tokenizer methods may discard teacher probability mass or assign it to student tokens with unrelated content. We introduce Byte-Prefix Marginalization (BPM), which re-expresses the teacher's next-token distribution over the student vocabulary in a shared byte space. Specifically, BPM assigns each teacher token's probability to the longest student token whose byte representation is a prefix of the teacher token's bytes, aggregates mass mapped to the same student token, and places otherwise unmatched mass in an explicit residual category. This produces a vocabulary-complete, byte-aligned, and mass-preserving target for dense OPD. The target exactly recovers the teacher-induced byte-prefix marginal when the relevant prefix does not span multiple teacher tokens (a condition satisfied at more than 99% of training positions) and uses a mass-preserving, chain-factorized lower bound otherwise. Across Qwen3-32B, GLM-Z1-9B-0414, and MiniMax-M2.7 as teachers, BPM consistently outperforms current cross-tokenizer methods on six mathematics and programming benchmarks, improving six-benchmark avg@8 by 3.7-6.6 points over the strongest baselines.

items.title: Researchers propose SPRO framework for process reinforcement learning that derives intrinsic process rewards and redefines step-wise advantage, improving training efficiency and accuracy without extra computational cost [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Self-Guided Process Reward Optimization with Redefined Step-wise Advantage for Process Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Researchers introduce Self-Guided Process Reward Optimization (SPRO), a novel framework for process reinforcement learning that derives process rewards intrinsically from the policy model and redefines step-wise advantage using Cumulative Process Rewards and Masked Step Advantage. SPRO outperforms vanilla GRPO with 3.4 times higher training efficiency and a 12.9% improvement in test accuracy while maintaining stable policy entropy and reducing response length. The framework achieves these gains without additional computational overhead compared to existing outcome-supervised reinforcement learning methods, supporting its potential for industrial applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2507.01551v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Process Reinforcement Learning~(PRL) has demonstrated considerable potential in enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models~(LLMs). However, introducing additional process reward models incurs substantial computational overhead, and there is no unified theoretical framework for process-level advantage estimation. To bridge this gap, we propose \textbf{S}elf-Guided \textbf{P}rocess \textbf{R}eward \textbf{O}ptimization~(\textbf{SPRO}), a novel framework that enables process-aware RL through two key innovations: (1) we show that process rewards can be derived intrinsically from the policy model itself, and (2) we redefine step-wise advantage by introducing well-defined Cumulative Process Rewards~(\textbf{CPR}) and \textbf{M}asked \textbf{S}tep \textbf{A}dvantage~(\textbf{MSA}), which facilitates rigorous step-wise action advantage estimation within shared-prompt sampling groups. Our experimental results show that SPRO outperforms vanilla GRPO with 3.4x higher training efficiency and a 12.9\% test accuracy improvement. Furthermore, SPRO maintains a stable and elevated policy entropy throughout training while achieving a considerable reduction in response length, evidencing sufficient exploration and prevention of reward hacking. Notably, SPRO incurs no additional computational overhead compared to outcome-supervised RL methods such as GRPO, which benefit industrial implementation.

items.title: Researchers find that larger language models compound mistakes faster despite improved accuracy, revealing a self-perpetuating failure mode invisible to the models themselves [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reliability Scales Inversely: Bigger Language Models Compound Mistakes Faster
items.summary: A study analyzing three families of language models shows that as models scale, their knowledge gaps decrease but the rate of knowledge degradation and error compounding increases significantly. The researchers identify a causal mechanism where models commit to low-probability tokens and then condition subsequent outputs on these errors, leading to a snowball effect that persists even when the model's own uncertainty signals diminish. This failure mode evades self-monitoring tools and results in more frequent fabrications despite higher confidence levels. The findings highlight a trade-off between capability and reliability in larger language models and suggest that current approaches to improving model accuracy may overlook this inherent risk.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.18292v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As language models scale, answers start truer but degrade faster: scaling buys capability but erodes reliability. The knowledge-gap account -- more data, retrieval, or scale -- misses an auto-regressive risk residual that increases with scale: the model commits to a low-probability token, conditions on it as established, and snowballs. We track this through per-position disagreement $\delta = \log p_M - \log p_O$ against a stronger same-family oracle, whose second moment splits exactly into bias$^2$ $\mathrm{KL}(p_M \,\|\, p_O)^2$ and risk $\mathrm{Var}[\delta]$. Across three model families, we present four findings: (i) under scaling, the knowledge gap falls up to $7\times$ while knowledge degradation grows up to $39\times$; (ii) at a fabrication, felt uncertainty $H(p_M)$ relaxes quickly while oracle-referenced risk persists up to $23\times$ longer, leaving a confident-but-precarious risk regime that bridges consecutive fabrications; (iii) this regime is causal -- a fixed-$\mathrm{KL}$ variance contraction cuts web-verified hallucination $35$-$74\%$; and, (iv) it evades self-monitoring, with $p_M$-only detectors (e.g. semantic entropy) firing $\approx$$30\%$ less ($p\!<\!10^{-16}$) on the risky branch despite it holding nearly $4\times$ more fabrications. Bigger models snowball mistakes faster, through a failure mode that is dominant, self-perpetuating, causal and invisible to the model itself.

items.title: Researchers introduce DFAH-Bench to measure observable instability in financial AI agent decisions, analyzing over 4,700 episodes across synthetic compliance and financial DataOps groups [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DFAH-Bench: Benchmarking Observable Agent Instability in Financial Decision-Making
items.summary: DFAH-Bench benchmarks the consistency of financial AI agents by assessing decision agreement and tool-path agreement during replay, highlighting variations in execution despite stable decisions. The study analyzed 4,157 retrospective episodes and 570 prospective episodes, revealing decision agreement rates above 94% but significant discrepancies in tool usage paths and argument-result trajectories. This approach aims to improve replay fidelity, investigation, and change control in AI-driven financial decision-making processes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.20491v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A financial AI agent can repeat a decision while changing the tools, order, or recorded arguments and results used to reach it. Outcome-only evaluation misses this variation, even when it matters for replay and change control. DFAH-Bench operationalizes the Determinism-Faithfulness Assurance Harness (DFAH), where faithfulness means fidelity of observable execution under replay, not answer correctness. The protocol qualifies comparable, sufficiently observed replays and measures decision agreement (DAR) and tool-path agreement (TAR) over the same eligible groups. We analyze 4,157 retrospective episodes from configurations with observed tool use across 719 synthetic compliance and financial DataOps groups, together with an argument-aware prospective extension comprising 570 eligible episodes across 190 groups. In that extension, decisions agree 94.2-95.1% while exact tool-name paths agree 66.9-69.4%, producing 25.8-27.3 percentage-point gaps; argument-and-result trajectory agreement falls to 45.0-51.5%. Even among unanimous-decision groups, paths vary in 66.7-68.9% under task weighting. DFAH-Bench makes the execution behind a stable decision visible for replay, investigation, and change review.

items.title: Researchers propose Adversarial Style Optimization to enhance visual jailbreak attacks on Multimodal Large Language Models by exploiting stylistic vulnerabilities using GRPO-based image editing [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Adversarial Style Optimization: Enhancing VLM Jailbreaks by GRPO-based Stylistic Triggers Optimization
items.summary:
A recent study introduces Adversarial Style Optimization (ASO), a method that improves jailbreak attacks on Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by targeting stylistic weaknesses rather than content. The researchers found that while MLLMs understand content across various visual styles, their safety mechanisms can be bypassed by specific stylistic triggers. ASO fine-tunes an image-editing model with a Group Relative Policy Optimization agent and a reward function combining refusal detection and semantic evaluation to optimize stylistic modifications on adversarial images.

Experiments show that ASO significantly increases the success rate of state-of-the-art visual jailbreak attacks, revealing stylistic biases as a scalable vulnerability for testing MLLM security. The researchers have made the ASO code publicly available for further study and development.

items.originalTitle: Probing Latent Colombian Identity Inferences in Qwen2.5-7B with Natural Language Autoencoders
items.summary: A pilot study investigates whether the large language model Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct internally encodes Colombian identity, socioeconomic status, or stereotypes when processing Colombian-Spanish and English prompts. The research uses Natural Language Autoencoders to analyze activations from a specific model layer across 30 prompts with explicit, implicit, and neutral Colombian cues. The study offers descriptive and qualitative insights into latent nationality and stereotype representations within the model before these appear in its outputs, contributing to understanding bias and interpretability in language models for underrepresented Spanish dialects.

items.originalTitle: Khondo: A Multimodal Benchmark for Document Packet Splitting of Bangla Forms
items.summary: Researchers have developed Khondo, the first benchmark dataset for splitting document packets of Bangladeshi government forms that operates directly on bilingual (Bangla-English) page images. The dataset covers five concatenation schemes across 14 administrative domains with annotated boundaries and page orders, enabling evaluation of document clustering and page ordering tasks. Evaluations show models can cluster pages into original documents but struggle to restore correct page order, especially when pages are shuffled. The study identifies page-order reconstruction as a key challenge in vision-based document understanding for low-resource languages and provides Khondo as a resource to advance research in this area.

items.title: Researchers introduce J-CoT, a recurrent reasoning framework using vocabulary-indexed J-space to improve language model reasoning without full verbalization of intermediate steps [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: J-CoT: Chain-of-Thought in J-Space
items.summary: Researchers have developed J-CoT, a new reasoning framework that operates within a vocabulary-indexed coordinate system called J-space to carry intermediate reasoning states as J-thoughts. This approach avoids the need for fully verbalized intermediate rationales and does not require recurrence over the entire hidden state, enabling more efficient reasoning in language models. Evaluations show that J-CoT-Zero matches or surpasses existing latent-reasoning baselines, while J-CoT-Train achieves top scores across mathematical, scientific, coding, and structured path-reasoning benchmarks.

items.originalSummary: Researchers have introduced J-CoT, a new recurrent reasoning framework designed to improve language model reasoning. Unlike traditional chain-of-thought prompting that relies solely on natural language for intermediate steps, J-CoT operates within a vocabulary-indexed coordinate system called J-space. This approach allows the model to carry intermediate reasoning states as vocabulary-indexed coefficients, termed J-thoughts, which are then mapped back into the model's hidden representations for subsequent reasoning cycles. This method avoids the need for fully verbalized intermediate rationales and does not require recurrence over the entire hidden state. Evaluations show that J-CoT-Zero matches or surpasses existing latent-reasoning baselines, while J-CoT-Train achieves the highest scores across various mathematical, scientific, coding, and structured path-reasoning benchmarks.

items.title: Study benchmarks fine-tuning and retrieval strategies for Gemma 4 31B multimodal model on NRC Reactor Operator licensing exams, achieving near 80% accuracy on 8 of 14 tests [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Benchmarking Fine-tuning and Retrieval Strategies for a Multimodal Language Model on the NRC Reactor Operator Licensing Examination
items.summary:
A recent study evaluated the 31-billion-parameter multimodal language model Gemma 4 31B-IT on the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission Reactor Operator licensing examination, benchmarking eight configurations combining fine-tuning and retrieval strategies. The fine-tuned model with fixed-size chunking retrieval met the human passing criterion on 8 out of 14 exams, reaching an aggregate accuracy close to 80%. No configuration without fine-tuning passed any exam.
The research compared supervised fine-tuning with chain-of-thought rationales, retrieval-augmented generation using domain-specific documents, and retrieval-augmented fine-tuning, also analyzing fixed-size sliding-window chunking versus structure-aware chunking. Results showed that chunking strategy effectiveness depends on the model's training state, and retrieval-augmented fine-tuning underperformed standard fine-tuning. These findings inform effective integration of large language models into nuclear industry applications requiring specialized knowledge.

items.originalTitle: FSE: Continual Learning for Named Entity Recognition by Fast-Slow Experts
items.summary: The FSE (Fast-Slow Experts) model addresses challenges in continual learning for named entity recognition by using a fast expert to filter unlikely token spans and a slow expert to classify remaining spans, reducing catastrophic forgetting and enhancing knowledge sharing. A length-decay negative sampling strategy is also introduced to mitigate span imbalance. Experiments demonstrate that FSE achieves faster convergence and improved performance compared to existing methods on benchmark datasets.

items.originalSummary: A new model called FSE (Fast-Slow Experts) has been proposed to improve Continual Learning for Named Entity Recognition (CLNER). Additionally, a length-decay negative sampling strategy is introduced to handle span imbalance. Experiments on OntoNotes and FewNERD datasets show that FSE achieves state-of-the-art results, faster convergence, and effective knowledge sharing across tasks.

items.title: Researchers introduce a multilayer taxonomy of 14 capability domains and 91 subskills for large language models, analyzing 15,934 papers from 2023 to 2025 to map research focus areas [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Isolated Tasks to Structured Capabilities: A Multilayer Taxonomy for Large Language Models
items.summary: Researchers have developed a multilayer taxonomy to classify large language model (LLM) capabilities into 14 domains and 91 subskills, moving beyond isolated task evaluations to structured capability analysis. They applied this taxonomy to 15,934 LLM-focused papers from major AI conferences between 2023 and 2025, revealing concentrated research on Language-Semantic Competence, Reasoning, Planning and Decision-Making, and Perception, while several domains received minimal attention. This taxonomy, guided by human cognitive science rather than LLM architecture, aims to improve research organization, identify coverage gaps, and support evaluation and training strategies by shifting the focus from tasks to capabilities.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.22182v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) evaluation spans diverse tasks and benchmarks, yet evidence remains organized around tasks rather than the capabilities they probe. This fragmentation limits cross-study comparison, obscures capabilities tasks recruit, and makes coverage gaps difficult to identify. We introduce a multi-layer taxonomy of 14 capability domains and 91 subskills across Primitive, Constructed, and Integrative layers. Human cognitive science guides capability definition and organization, not LLM architecture. Layer assignments draw on developmental precedence and hypothesized functional support, while human-origin constructs are adapted to observable model behavior. To demonstrate operational utility, we screened 31,505 papers from ACL, AAAI, ICML, and NeurIPS between 2023 and 2025 and mapped 15,934 LLM-focused papers through multi-model annotation, consensus, and arbitration. Direct research attention concentrated on Language-Semantic Competence (3,551; 22.3%), Reasoning (3,388; 21.3%), Planning and Decision-Making (2,149; 13.5%), and Perception (1,954; 12.3%), whereas six domains appeared in fewer than 2% of papers. Within domains, the most frequent subskill had a median prevalence of 97.9% and appeared in at least 90% of papers in 10 of 14 domains. Language-Semantic Competence and Reasoning formed the highest-volume pair (n = 1,864; 11.7%; lift = 2.47), whereas Theory of Mind and Social Reasoning and Interaction showed the highest lift among pairs with at least 20 co-occurrences (n = 62; lift = 30.84). By shifting the unit of analysis from isolated tasks to structured capabilities, the taxonomy supports research organization, coverage audits, evaluation interpretation, and testable hypotheses for diagnosis, training, and transfer.

items.title: Researchers analyze when large language models align with or diverge from human creativity evaluations, finding differences in sensitivity to novelty and contextual information [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Why Large Language Models and Humans Converge and Diverge in Evaluating Creativity
items.summary:
Researchers conducted three studies using six widely used large language models (LLMs) to examine how their creativity evaluations compare to human judgments. They found that LLMs generally rely on a narrower set of creativity standards, aligning most closely with humans on novelty but diverging on contextual factors like social and market information. Each LLM applied distinct evaluation standards, affecting their creativity judgments.

The studies showed that LLM evaluations moderately correlated with human ratings, with models using broader standards better distinguishing more creative ideas. However, LLMs were less sensitive to contextual information that significantly influenced human creativity assessments. These findings suggest that alignment between LLM and human creativity evaluations depends on the type of evidence considered and the specific standards each model uses, making the choice of LLM evaluator important for recognizing creative ideas.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.22218v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite the growing use of large language models (LLMs) as creativity evaluators, evidence of their alignment with human evaluations remains mixed, raising the question of when and why their judgments converge with or diverge from human judgments. Across three studies and six widely used LLMs, we addressed this gap by identifying the standards underlying LLM creativity evaluation and examining their downstream implications. Study 1 showed that LLMs generally relied on a narrower subset of human creativity evaluation standards. Convergence with human standards was strongest in the novelty dimension, whereas divergence was clearest in the contextual dimension, which captures social, market, and reputational information. Moreover, each LLM exhibited distinct, model-specific standards that varied substantially in breadth. These differences in evaluation standards were reflected in actual creativity judgments. Study 2 (N = 1,103 ideas) showed that LLM evaluations were moderately correlated with human evaluations, and individual LLMs with broader standards better distinguished ideas humans judged as more versus less creative. Study 3 (N = 1,195) showed that LLMs were less sensitive to contextual information: such information significantly altered human creativity ratings but left LLM ratings largely unchanged. Together, our findings help explain the mixed evidence on LLM-human alignment, showing that alignment depends on the evidence a judgment demands and the standards each model applies. LLMs may resemble humans when evaluations emphasize intrinsic qualities such as novelty, yet diverge when judgments require contextual information. Selecting an LLM evaluator is therefore a consequential decision: different models, applying different standards, recognize different ideas as creative.

items.title: Survey finds organizations lack systematic processes to validate EU AI Act requirements in requirements engineering; experts see promise and risks in LLM-based validation tools [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: From Obligation to Specification: A Survey on Validating EU AI Act Requirements in RE
items.summary: A study involving expert interviews and surveys reveals that many organizations developing or operating AI systems are unprepared to translate EU AI Act obligations into testable, auditable requirements and verifiable evidence. While the Act is considered highly relevant, structured mechanisms for capturing regulatory obligations, updating projects, and maintaining traceability are often missing. Participants from requirements engineering, data science, development, and compliance roles view large language model-based agentic validation tools as promising for mapping obligations to requirements and organizing evidence but express concerns about full automation and emphasize the need for safeguards. The study outlines minimum requirements for a closed-loop approach to meet EU AI Act compliance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.21608v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: With the EU AI Act entering into force, organizations developing or operating AI systems face new obligations on transparency, risk management, and traceability. For Requirements Engineering (RE), these obligations must be translated into testable, auditable requirements and verifiable evidence. However, many organizations currently lack systematic processes to achieve this. We hypothesize that LLM-based agentic validation tools can support this translation, thereby helping to close this gap. We present a mixed-method exploratory study with expert interviews (N=10) and an online survey (N=15) to assess organizational preparedness for EU AI Act-oriented RE and perceptions of LLM-based, agentic closed-loop validation tools, with participants spanning RE, data science, development, and compliance roles. Our results show that, although the EU AI Act is viewed as highly relevant, structured mechanisms to capture regulatory obligations, propagate updates into projects, and maintain lifecycle-wide traceability and evidence are often missing. Participants see LLM-based tools as promising for mapping obligations to requirements, assessing coverage, and organizing evidence, but express strong concerns about full automation and stress the need for safeguards. Based on these findings, we outline minimum requirements for an EU AI Act-ready closed-loop approach.

items.title: Researchers identify the Hard Decision Layer in transformers where answer rankings stabilize abruptly during inference, improving accuracy across multiple language models and datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Hard Decision Layer: Evidence for Committed Inference in Transformers
items.summary: Researchers investigated how transformer-based language models commit to predictions in multiple-choice question answering and identified a Hard Decision Layer (HDL), a natural architectural feature where answer rankings stabilize abruptly during inference. This phenomenon was consistently observed across four language models—Qwen, Llama, Granite, and Mistral—and four benchmark datasets, without requiring learned routing policies or being affected by fine-tuning. The HDL corresponds with significant accuracy improvements, such as a 0.61 increase for Qwen on CommonsenseQA, after which performance stabilizes. Systematic tests confirmed that the HDL is a fundamental property of transformer architecture. These findings provide mechanistic insights into transformer inference and suggest potential for more efficient reasoning and model steering.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.21613v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate where and how transformer-based language models commit to predictions in multiple-choice question answering. We identify the _Hard Decision Layer_ (HDL), a natural architectural property where answer option rankings stabilize abruptly during inference. Empirical validation across four language models (Qwen, Llama, Granite, Mistral) and four benchmark datasets demonstrates consistent HDL emergence without learned routing policies. We also show that the HDL is invariant to fine-tuning. Our results reveal striking accuracy improvements at the HDL: up to +0.61 (Qwen on CommonsenseQA), after which performance stabilizes. Systematic ablations on label formats and problem complexity confirm the phenomenon is fundamental to model architecture. These findings offer mechanistic insights into transformer inference and suggest opportunities for efficient reasoning and model steering. All code and results required to reproduce this work are available in https://github.com/Mystic-Slice/hard-decision-layer

items.title: Researchers introduce FaithC4 benchmark to evaluate transcription faithfulness of vision-language models versus traditional OCR across English, Chinese, and Korean documents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Do VLMs Read or Rewrite? On Transcription Faithfulness in Vision-Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have found that vision-language models (VLMs) used for document understanding often rewrite imperfect text into more plausible forms rather than transcribing faithfully, a behavior undetected by standard OCR benchmarks. They introduced FaithC4, a multilingual benchmark with 1,455 single-page documents in English, Chinese, and Korean, containing three types of text perturbations to test transcription accuracy across 15 systems including general-purpose VLMs, OCR-specialized VLMs, and traditional OCR pipelines.

The study revealed that general-purpose VLMs experience up to 4.5 points degradation in word error rate under perturbations, OCR-specialized VLMs degrade by 0.2 to 2 points, and traditional OCR pipelines degrade less than 0.6 points on English documents. Analysis of the Qwen3-VL-4B model showed that rewriting occurs when the model's internal representation of a perturbed word remains close to the original, while significant divergence leads to faithful transcription. Additionally, shorter words (4-6 characters) are rewritten up to 10% of the time, with rewriting dropping sharply for words longer than eight characters.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.21617v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly used in place of traditional OCR pipelines for document understanding. In this paper, we show they do not always act as faithful transcribers: when text is imperfect, they often tend to rewrite it into a more plausible form - a behavior that clean-text OCR benchmarks cannot detect. We introduce FaithC4, a multilingual perturbation benchmark of 1,455 single-page documents (English, Chinese, Korean) with three perturbation families: scramble, random substitution, and visually similar substitution. We use the benchmark to evaluate 15 systems spanning general-purpose VLMs, OCR-specialized VLMs, and traditional OCR pipelines. These three categories differ in WER degradation under perturbation: general-purpose VLMs degrade by up to 4.5 points, OCR-specialized VLMs by 0.2-2 points, and traditional OCR by less than 0.6 points on English. Probing Qwen3-VL-4B layer-by-layer, we identify a consistent pattern: rewriting fires only when a perturbed word's final layer FFN representation stays close to the original encoding; when the representation diverges sufficiently, the model transcribes faithfully. Word length affects rewriting rate: short words (4-6 characters) are rewritten up to 10% of the time, with a sharp cutoff at 8 characters above which rewriting drops to 0%.

items.title: NVIDIA releases Molt, a PyTorch-native training framework for agentic reinforcement learning with asynchronous multimodal policy training [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Molt: A Scalable PyTorch-Native Training Framework for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: NVIDIA has introduced Molt, a scalable PyTorch-native training framework designed to simplify agentic reinforcement learning research by reducing the complexity of algorithm modifications and pipeline changes. Molt features a compact, clean codebase that allows researchers and AI coding assistants to trace and modify algorithm flows end to end, supporting asynchronous training of multimodal and mixture-of-experts policies without training on tokens not generated by the model itself. The framework achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art Megatron-based stacks under fully asynchronous protocols and is available as open source with recipes and containers on GitHub.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.21653v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning research is constant algorithm modification, new estimators, new pipeline stages, new rollout schemes, and in mainstream frameworks each change threads through layers of trainer, distributed backend, and rollout glue: the cost lands on the researcher at every iteration. Molt is a PyTorch-native training framework built to keep that cost small: a codebase compact and clean enough for a researcher to hold in their head, and for an AI coding assistant to read and reason about in its entirety, so the algorithm flow can be traced and changed end to end. The agent is an ordinary program, and one asynchronous loop trains multimodal and mixture-of-experts policies while never training on a token it did not generate, consistent in tokens, policy versions, and model semantics. Leanness does not cost performance: under a matched, fully asynchronous protocol, Molt is statistically comparable to a state-of-the-art Megatron-based stack. Molt is open source and provides recipes and containers at https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/labs-molt.

items.title: Researchers find causal evidence sets outperform attention-based training for sparse attention routing in language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning What Matters: Supervising Sparse Attention Routing with Causal Evidence Sets
items.summary: Researchers tested the assumption that attention patterns reveal the context a model uses by comparing attention with causal dependence on retrieval tasks where evidence is known. They found that attention often disagrees with causal dependence, with models attending to outdated facts and varying attention across runs, leading to lower accuracy when training selectors on attention alone. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.21692v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse attention reduces the cost of long contexts by allowing each query to read only selected parts of the input. These selectors are often trained by distilling the attention patterns of a dense teacher, assuming that attention reveals which context the teacher actually uses. We test that assumption on retrieval tasks where the evidence for each answer is known exactly. By masking parts of the context and measuring whether the answer changes, we find that attention and causal dependence often disagree, and distilled selectors inherit the mismatch. Teachers attend to outdated facts they have learned to ignore, and their attention can vary across training runs even when they rely on the same evidence. In a two-step reference task, attention at the answer skips the intermediate step because it was resolved earlier in the forward pass: a selector trained on attention achieves 41% accuracy, while the same selector trained on causal evidence reaches 99% and matches the teacher. These evidence sets require no annotation: recovered from a frozen teacher by masking alone, they train selectors to the same accuracy. We find the same conflict in pretrained models: Qwen2.5-3B gives more attention to an outdated fact than the current one on 58% of conflicting-fact examples despite answering correctly, while Gemma-2-9B rises from 56% to 99% accuracy when restricted to the two relevant sentences. Attention shows where a model looks, not necessarily what its answer depends on; across the regimes we tested, that dependence matched or outperformed attention as a training target.

items.title: Researchers introduce ADSD, a prompt-suffix attack that disrupts verifier acceptance in speculative decoding, increasing sample time by 62.3% on GSM8K while preserving task quality [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Adversarial Prompts for Acceptance Collapse in Speculative Decoding
items.summary:
Researchers have identified a vulnerability in lossless acceleration schemes like speculative decoding, which rely on token-level alignment between draft and target models for faster inference. They introduced ADSD, the first prompt-suffix attack that collapses verifier acceptance by shifting draft probability toward tokens unlikely to be accepted by the target model, thereby undermining the alignment guarantee.

ADSD employs Soft-Collapse, a surrogate aligned with the verifier's asymmetric acceptance rule, combined with a target-preservation objective to avoid obvious task corruption. The attack significantly increases mean sample time by 62.3% on the GSM8K dataset without degrading task performance. The study also demonstrates that this vulnerability spans multiple domains, speculative decoding methods, and model architectures, highlighting a broad operational risk in current acceleration techniques.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.21804v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Lossless acceleration schemes, such as speculative decoding, promise significant inference speedups by relying on dynamic token-level alignment between a draft and a target model. However, this guarantee of semantic equivalence masks a severe operational vulnerability: draft-target alignment can be systematically attacked. In this paper, we introduce ADSD, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first prompt-suffix attack that collapses verifier acceptance by pushing draft probability mass toward tokens the target is unlikely to accept. ADSD uses Soft-Collapse, a verifier-aligned surrogate derived from the asymmetric speculative acceptance rule, together with a target-preservation objective that discourages obvious task corruption. ADSD successfully generates highly effective adversarial suffixes. On the GSM8K dataset, our attack increases the mean sample time by 62.3% while preserving the task quality. We further show that this vulnerability exists across different domains, speculative decoding strategies, and model architectures.

items.originalTitle: Zero-Shot Mission-Level Evaluation for Aerial MLLM Agents
items.summary: Researchers have developed MissionBench, a benchmark designed to assess the ability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to perform long-horizon embodied tasks in aerial 3D environments using only egocentric observations and action history without fine-tuning. The benchmark includes 120 missions across five simulated environments and four task families, requiring agents to autonomously plan, navigate, and report outcomes from a single high-level instruction. Evaluation of 22 open- and closed-source MLLMs showed the best model succeeded in fewer than 35% of missions, compared to 84.4% human performance, highlighting the challenge of multi-step embodied tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.22014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are emerging as core reasoning modules for embodied agents, yet it remains unclear how well general-purpose models can solve long-horizon embodied tasks from a single high-level instruction. We introduce MissionBench, a benchmark for mission-level evaluation of MLLMs in aerial 3D environments. It comprises 120 missions across five simulated 3D environments and four task families. Agents must autonomously plan, navigate, and report outcomes using only egocentric observations and its action history, without aerial-specific fine-tuning. Across 22 open- and closed-source MLLMs, the strongest model succeeds on fewer than 35% of missions compared to 84.4% human performance, highlighting the difficulty of multi-step embodied tasks. Despite large variations between model families, we observe gains from scaling, indicating that larger general-purpose models possess stronger zero-shot embodied capabilities. Our analysis shows that mission-level competence requires coordinating multiple capabilities beyond spatial perception, including multi-step planning and adaptive reasoning. This motivates closed-loop evaluation and highlights both the promise and risk of scaling-driven improvements for embodied AI.

items.title: Study finds small vision-language models internally detect errors better than their verbalized confidence under image degradation but fail under severe low-light conditions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Small Vision-Language Models Know When They Are Wrong But Cannot Say So: A Two-Model Study of Stated versus Internal Confidence Under Realistic Image Degradation
items.summary: Researchers evaluated two small open-weight vision-language models, Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct and SmolVLM-Instruct, across six types of realistic image degradations at varying severity levels to compare their verbalized confidence against internal token probability as measures of uncertainty. They found that while the models' verbalized confidence was often constant or unavailable and poorly correlated with actual errors, the internal token probability reliably distinguished correct from incorrect answers except under severe underexposure where accuracy and error detection collapsed. The study concludes that these models possess usable self-knowledge not expressed in their verbal output, making internal probability a better signal for deferral decisions in constrained deployments, though neither confidence measure is reliable in extreme low-light scenarios.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.22034v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed on consumer hardware where input images are degraded by compression, camera shake, and poor lighting. In such settings, a reliable uncertainty signal matters more than raw accuracy, because it determines when a system should defer rather than answer. We evaluate two small open-weight VLMs -- Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct and SmolVLM-Instruct -- across six realistic photographic degradations at three severity levels, comparing two confidence signals: the confidence the model states in natural language, and the model's own mean token probability over its generated answer. Across 3,800 predictions, we find a large and consistent gap. Verbalized confidence in Qwen2-VL is almost constant (mean 0.87-0.90 across all conditions) and detects its own errors at chance level (AUROC 0.39-0.75, typically ~0.50), while internal token probability from the same model separates correct from incorrect answers with AUROC 0.92-0.99. In SmolVLM, verbalized confidence proved largely unobtainable: across three prompt templates, only one of five pilot attempts produced a parseable confidence value, while internal probability again yielded above-chance error detection (AUROC 0.54-0.92). Both models fail in the same place: under severe underexposure, accuracy collapses (0.99->0.22 for Qwen2-VL, 0.97->0.42 for SmolVLM) while both confidence signals barely move, and internal error-detection falls to chance. We conclude that small VLMs encode usable self-knowledge that their verbalized output does not express, that internal probability is therefore the better deferral signal in constrained deployment, and that neither signal should be trusted under severe low-light conditions.

items.title: Nanbeige4.2-3B launches as a compact 3B-parameter agentic model outperforming larger models on diverse benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Nanbeige4.2-3B: Unlocking Agentic Capabilities in a Compact Mode
items.summary: Nanbeige4.2-3B is a compact general agentic model with 3 billion non-embedding parameters that delivers strong performance on code-agent, office-agent, and complex tool-use tasks while maintaining competitive reasoning in mathematics, coding, and science. It is pretrained from scratch on 28 trillion tokens using a Looped Transformer architecture that increases capacity without adding parameters. The model's training pipeline includes mixed-mode reinforcement learning with human feedback and agentic reinforcement learning to improve quality and stability. Evaluations show Nanbeige4.2-3B outperforms larger models such as Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma4-12B across various agentic benchmarks and remains competitive on reasoning and alignment tasks. Its performance with OpenClaw supports its use as a compact local personal assistant.

items.title: Researchers find LLMs' validation of pseudo-science varies widely by deployment configuration, with Grok showing inconsistent credibility scores across interfaces and updates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Opaque Epistemic Mediation: How LLM Deployment Configurations Shape the Validation of Pseudo-Science
items.summary: A study tested four major large language models (Claude, Grok, GPT, Gemini) on their evaluation of ethnonationalist pseudo-science claims over several months, revealing significant variability in credibility scores depending on deployment settings. Grok's Fast versions assigned much higher credibility than others, and silent updates and interface differences caused drastic changes in outputs without public disclosure. The study highlights that an LLM's epistemic stance is not inherent but shaped by system prompts, safety layers, and deployment choices, which remain opaque to users and researchers. The authors call for new forms of epistemic accountability to address this public concern.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.22513v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Commercial large language models are increasingly used as knowledge references, yet their stance on contested scientific claims is neither stable nor transparent. We tested how four major LLM families (Claude, Grok, GPT, Gemini) evaluate ethnonationalist pseudo-science derived from Frank Salter's biosocial framework across four temporal snapshots (October 2025-February 2026), via both API and web interfaces. Grok's Fast versions (which power the default user experience on X) consistently assigned credibility scores of 70-75, two to five times higher than all other models (which scored 15-40). This pattern was absent from control prompts testing basic evolutionary consensus and refuted Lamarckian claims, where all models performed comparably. Three additional findings emerged: (1) a silent patch reversed Grok's behaviour from chaotic to stably high validation overnight, without any public documentation; (2) the same Grok model identifier produced radically divergent outputs via API (75) and web (5.5) three months later; (3) refusal to rate the pseudo-scientific claim, the most defensible response observed, appeared in two model families through different interfaces (Claude Opus 4.1 categorically via web, GPT-5.1 Chat intermittently via API) and eroded in the successor version of each. These results indicate that the epistemic stance of a commercial LLM is not a stable property of the model but a contingent effect of deployment configuration: system prompts, safety layers, interface routing, and silent updates. This remains opaque to users and researchers alike. We argue this constitutes a matter of public concern requiring new forms of epistemic accountability.

items.title: Researchers evaluate nine LLMs in morally charged social dilemmas, finding inconsistent moral behavior influenced by game structure and framing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Ethics and Payoffs Diverge: LLM Agents in Morally Charged Social Dilemmas
items.summary: Researchers introduced a framework to assess how large language models (LLMs) behave in social dilemmas where ethical considerations conflict with profit incentives, such as the prisoner's dilemma and public goods game. They tested nine models across varying moral contexts, opponent behaviors, and survival pressures, analyzing both behavior and reasoning to understand motives behind decisions. The study found cooperation rates varied widely from 7.9% to 76.3%, with no model consistently acting morally. Game structure and moral framing were the strongest factors affecting moral behavior, while reasoning traces revealed motives ranging from payoff-maximizing to moral and reputation-oriented. These findings highlight the situational fragility of current LLMs' ethical behavior and caution against deploying them where profit conflicts with ethical guidelines.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2505.19212v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent advances in LLMs have enabled their use in complex agentic roles, involving decision-making with humans or other agents, making ethical alignment a critical concern. While prior work has examined LLMs' moral judgment and strategic behavior separately, there is limited understanding of how they act when moral imperatives directly conflict with profit incentives. We introduce \msimfull (\msim) to evaluate how LLMs behave in the prisoner's dilemma and public goods game embedded in morally charged contexts, varying moral framing, opponent behavior, and survival pressure across nine models. Beyond measuring behavior, we estimate the causal effect of each factor via average treatment effects (ATEs) and analyze agents' own reasoning traces to characterize the motives behind their choices. We find that no model remains consistently moral, with cooperation rates ranging from 7.9\% to 76.3\%. Game structure and moral framing are the strongest causal drivers of moral behavior, while reasoning-trace analysis reveals distinct motive profiles across models, ranging from predominantly payoff-maximizing to moral- and reputation-oriented. Together, these results expose the situational brittleness of current LLMs' moral behavior and the risk of deploying them where profit incentives conflict with ethical guidelines.

items.title: MedKGent framework uses LLM agents to build a temporally evolving medical knowledge graph from over 10 million PubMed abstracts, creating the largest LLM-derived medical KG to date [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MedKGent: A Large Language Model Agent Framework for Constructing Temporally Evolving Medical Knowledge Graph
items.summary:
MedKGent is a Large Language Model agent framework designed to construct a medical knowledge graph that evolves over time by processing more than 10 million PubMed abstracts from 1975 to 2023. It employs two specialized agents: an Extractor Agent that identifies knowledge triples with confidence scores, and a Constructor Agent that integrates these triples into a temporal graph, reinforcing recurring information and resolving conflicts. The resulting knowledge graph contains 156,275 entities and nearly 3 million triples, with automated and expert evaluations showing about 90% validity for the extracted triples.

In downstream tests, the MedKGent knowledge graph improved retrieval-augmented generation performance across five large language models on seven medical question-answering benchmarks. This positions MedKGent as a scalable and temporally aware infrastructure for representing medical knowledge and supporting AI research grounded in medical literature.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2508.12393v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The rapid expansion of medical literature challenges the scalable structuring of domain knowledge. Knowledge Graphs (KGs) offer a solution, yet current construction methods lack generalizability and ignore the temporal dynamics of evolving knowledge. To address this, we introduce MedKGent, a Large Language Model (LLM) agent framework for building temporally evolving medical KGs. Using over 10 million PubMed abstracts from 1975 to 2023, MedKGent incrementally constructs a KG daily via two specialized agents. The Extractor Agent identifies knowledge triples and assigns confidence scores, while the Constructor Agent integrates these triples into a temporal graph, reinforcing recurring knowledge and resolving conflicts. The resulting KG contains 156,275 entities and 2,971,384 triples, making it, to our knowledge, the largest LLM-derived medical KG to date. Automated and expert assessments showed triple-validity rates approaching 90%. In downstream evaluations, MedKGent-KG significantly improved retrieval-augmented generation for five LLMs across seven medical question-answering benchmarks. Together, these results position MedKGent as a scalable and temporally aware infrastructure for medical knowledge representation and literature-grounded AI research.

items.title: Researchers introduce InteractComp benchmark to evaluate search agents' ability to handle ambiguous queries through interaction, revealing low accuracy and stagnated interaction capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: InteractComp: Evaluating Search Agents With Ambiguous Queries
items.summary:
Researchers have developed InteractComp, a benchmark designed to test whether search agents can detect ambiguous user queries and actively interact to clarify them during search. The benchmark includes 210 expert-curated questions across nine domains that require interaction to resolve ambiguity. Evaluation of 17 models showed the best achieved only 13.73% accuracy on ambiguous queries, despite 71.50% accuracy with complete context, indicating overconfidence rather than reasoning flaws.

The study found that forcing interaction significantly improved performance, demonstrating latent capabilities that current strategies fail to utilize. A longitudinal analysis revealed that while search performance improved seven-fold over 15 months, interaction abilities stagnated, highlighting a critical blind spot in search agent development. InteractComp offers a valuable resource for evaluating and training interactive capabilities in search agents, with code publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2510.24668v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language agents have demonstrated remarkable potential in web search and information retrieval. However, many search-agent benchmarks assume that user queries are complete and unambiguous. This assumption leaves under-tested a practical failure mode: agents may face ambiguous requests where the intended target cannot be identified without clarification. Yet most agents lack interactive mechanisms during the search process, and existing benchmarks cannot assess this capability. To address this gap, we introduce InteractComp, a benchmark designed to evaluate whether search agents can recognize query ambiguity and actively interact to resolve it during search. Following the principle of easy to verify, interact to disambiguate, we construct 210 expert-curated questions across 9 domains through a target-distractor methodology that creates controlled ambiguity resolvable only through interaction. Evaluation of 17 models reveals striking failure: the best model achieves only 13.73% accuracy despite 71.50% with complete context, exposing systematic overconfidence rather than reasoning deficits. Forced interaction produces dramatic gains, demonstrating latent capability current strategies fail to engage. Longitudinal analysis shows interaction capabilities stagnated over 15 months while search performance improved seven-fold, revealing a critical blind spot. This stagnation, coupled with the immediate feedback inherent to search tasks, makes InteractComp a valuable resource for both evaluating and training interaction capabilities in search agents. The code is available at https://github.com/FoundationAgents/InteractComp.

items.title: Researchers propose SwiftMem, a query-aware agentic memory system using temporal and semantic indexing to reduce retrieval latency for LLM agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SwiftMem: Fast Agentic Memory via Query-aware Indexing
items.summary: SwiftMem is designed to improve long-term context retrieval for large language model (LLM) agents by narrowing memory searches to query-relevant subsets using specialized temporal and semantic indexes. The system introduces a temporal index for efficient time-sensitive queries and a semantic DAG-Tag index that organizes topics hierarchically to map queries to relevant memory clusters. An embedding-tag co-consolidation mechanism addresses memory fragmentation by reorganizing storage based on semantic clusters to enhance locality. Evaluations on benchmarks like LoCoMo and LongMemEval show SwiftMem achieves search latencies around 10-13 milliseconds while maintaining competitive accuracy compared to existing HNSW-backed memory systems, offering an order-of-magnitude latency improvement on calibrated tests.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2601.08160v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agentic memory systems have become critical for enabling LLM agents to maintain long-term context and retrieve relevant information efficiently. However, existing memory frameworks often perform query-agnostic retrieval over the full memory embedding space even when their storage layer is backed by efficient vector indexes such as HNSW. This full-scope retrieval path creates latency bottlenecks as memory grows, hindering real-time agent interactions. We propose SwiftMem, a query-aware agentic memory system that narrows retrieval to query-relevant memory subsets through specialized indexing over temporal and semantic dimensions. Our temporal index enables logarithmic-time range queries for time-sensitive retrieval, while the semantic DAG-Tag index maps queries to relevant topics through hierarchical tag structures. To address memory fragmentation during growth, we introduce an embedding-tag co-consolidation mechanism that reorganizes storage based on semantic clusters to improve locality. Across LoCoMo and LongMemEval$_S$, SwiftMem reaches 10.8/12.7 ms search latency while maintaining competitive LLM-judge accuracy against strong HNSW-backed memory systems. On the calibrated benchmark, LoCoMo Refined, SwiftMem remains close to the top LLM-judge score while preserving an order-of-magnitude latency advantage.

items.title: Researchers present WHBench, a benchmark evaluating 22 large language models on 47 women's health scenarios with expert validation, revealing no model exceeds 75% accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: WHBench: Evaluating Frontier LLMs with Expert-in-the-Loop Validation on Women's Health Topics
items.summary:
Researchers developed the Women's Health Benchmark (WHBench), a suite of 47 expert-crafted scenarios across 10 women's health topics, to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on clinical accuracy, safety, equity, and guideline adherence. They assessed 22 models using a 23-criterion rubric and found that no model achieved more than 75 percent mean performance, with the best reaching 72.1 percent, highlighting significant gaps in fully correct responses and varying harm rates.

The evaluation included 3,102 attempted responses and applied safety-weighted penalties and server-side score recalculations. Inter-rater reliability was moderate at the response label level but high for model ranking, supporting WHBench's utility for comparative evaluation. The benchmark aims to expose clinically meaningful failure modes such as outdated guidelines, unsafe omissions, dosing errors, and equity-related blind spots, emphasizing the need for expert oversight in clinical deployment and providing a public tool to track safer, more equitable progress in women's health AI.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.00024v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used for medical guidance, but women's health remains under-evaluated in benchmark design. We present the Women's Health Benchmark (WHBench), a targeted evaluation suite of 47 expert-crafted scenarios across 10 women's health topics, designed to expose clinically meaningful failure modes including outdated guidelines, unsafe omissions, dosing errors, and equity-related blind spots. We evaluate 22 models using a 23-criterion rubric spanning clinical accuracy, completeness, safety, communication quality, instruction following, equity, uncertainty handling, and guideline adherence, with safety-weighted penalties and server-side score recalculation. Across 3,102 attempted responses (3,100 scored), no model mean performance exceeds 75 percent; the best model reaches 72.1 percent. Even top models show low fully correct rates and substantial variation in harm rates. Inter-rater reliability is moderate at the response label level but high for model ranking, supporting WHBench utility for comparative system evaluation while highlighting the need for expert oversight in clinical deployment. WHBench provides a public, failure-mode-aware benchmark to track safer and more equitable progress in womens health AI.

items.title: Researchers present SURE-RAG, a selective retrieval-augmented generation method that verifies evidence sufficiency and uncertainty for multi-hop question answering, achieving high accuracy on HotpotQA-RAG v3 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SURE-RAG: Sufficiency and Uncertainty-Aware Evidence Verification for Selective Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.summary: SURE-RAG is a new protocol designed to verify whether retrieved evidence sufficiently supports or refutes a candidate answer in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. It aggregates local relation distributions between claims and passages into interpretable features to make a three-way decision on evidence sufficiency, improving answer reliability by answering only when support is established. The method was evaluated on the HotpotQA-RAG v3 benchmark using an artifact-aware protocol and outperformed baseline models and a GPT-4o judge while remaining fully auditable. The study also highlights that sufficiency verification differs from hallucination detection, as shown by contrasting SURE-RAG with GPT-4o on unsafe detection tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.03534v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds answers in retrieved passages, yet relevance does not guarantee sufficiency: a topical passage may still fail to justify the answer. We study evidence sufficiency verification for selective RAG answering, in which a verifier receives a question, a candidate answer, and retrieved evidence and decides whether the evidence supports, refutes, or is insufficient for the answer, answering only when support is established. We present SURE-RAG, an aggregation protocol that treats evidence sufficiency as a set-level property: missing hops and unresolved conflicts cannot be detected by scoring passages independently. A shared claim-evidence verifier produces a local relation distribution for each (claim, passage) pair, which SURE-RAG aggregates into four interpretable answer-level feature blocks (coverage, relation strength, uncertainty, and retrieval), producing a three-way decision and an auditable selective score. We evaluate on HotpotQA-RAG v3, a controlled multi-hop benchmark, under an artifact-aware protocol (shortcut baselines, counterfactual swaps, no-oracle checks, and GPT-4o audits). Calibrated SURE-RAG attains 0.9075 Macro-F1 (raw 0.8951 +/- 0.0069), well above DeBERTa mean-pooling (0.6516) and a GPT-4o judge (0.7284), and on par with a strong concat cross-encoder (0.8888 +/- 0.0109) while remaining fully auditable. At 30% coverage, risk falls from 0.2588 to 0.1642, a 37% relative reduction. As a boundary-mapping experiment, we contrast SURE-RAG with GPT-4o on HaluBench unsafe detection: the ranking reverses (0.3343 vs. 0.7389 unsafe-F1), indicating that controlled sufficiency verification and natural hallucination detection are distinct problems.

It aggregates local relation distributions between claims and passages into interpretable features to make a three-way decision on evidence sufficiency, improving answer reliability by answering only when support is established. The method was evaluated on the HotpotQA-RAG v3 benchmark using an artifact-aware protocol and outperformed baseline models and a GPT-4o judge while remaining fully auditable. The study also highlights that sufficiency verification differs from hallucination detection, as shown by contrasting SURE-RAG with GPT-4o on unsafe detection tasks.

items.title: Gemma 4 introduces open-weight multimodal language models with dense and Mixture-of-Experts architectures from 2.3B to 31B parameters, featuring improved encoders and a thinking mode for reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Gemma 4 Technical Report
items.summary:
Gemma 4 is a new generation of open-weight, natively multimodal language models designed to enhance compute efficiency and reasoning capabilities. The model suite includes dense and Mixture-of-Experts architectures ranging from 2.3 billion to 31 billion parameters, with improved vision and audio encoders across all sizes and a unified, encoder-free architecture for the 12 billion parameter model that processes raw audio and image patches. It also integrates a thinking mode that allows the models to generate reasoning traces before responding.

The design improvements in Gemma 4 enhance inference speed, memory usage, compute efficiency, and long-context handling. The models demonstrate significant performance gains across STEM, multimodal, and long-context benchmarks, competing with larger, state-of-the-art open models in human-rated tasks.

items.title: Researchers propose Multi-Mask Diffusion Model to improve few-step language generation by preserving masking structure and enabling drafting capability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Multi-Mask Diffusion Language Models for Few-Step Generation
items.summary:
Researchers introduce the Multi-Mask Diffusion Model (MultiMDM) to address challenges in few-step generation with masked diffusion models (MDMs), which typically collapse to a fully masked state and lack terminal entropy for consistency. MultiMDM pushes each clean token toward a designated mask in the forward process, allowing the backward process to predict masks before refining tokens, enhancing generation quality and efficiency.

The team derives a closed-form ELBO training objective for MultiMDM that supports continual training from pretrained MDMs and develops a discrete-state consistency distillation scheme using shared-Gumbel coupling to reduce entropy. Experiments on pretraining and distillation demonstrate that MultiMDM provides an effective foundation for principled few-step language generation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.19686v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) are a promising family of language generators, but achieving high-quality few-step generation remains challenging. In MDMs, all forward trajectories collapse to a single fully masked state, leaving no terminal entropy for consistency-style few-step generation. While recent few-step alternatives based on uniform-state diffusion avoid this degeneracy, it becomes harder to distinguish clean tokens from noise than MDMs, which usually harms modeling quality and training efficiency. In this work, we propose a multi-mask diffusion model (MultiMDM) that preserves the masking structure towards few-step generation. In the forward process, each clean token is first pushed towards a designated mask and then gradually mixes over the mask set. As a result, the backward process has a drafting capability by predicting a designated mask before refining to a clean token. We derive a closed-form ELBO training objective for MultiMDM that supports continual training from pretrained MDMs. In addition, we formulate a purely discrete-state consistency distillation scheme, with a shared-Gumbel coupling to reduce pathwise entropy. Experiments on pretraining and distillation show that MultiMDM provides an effective foundation for principled few-step generation.
